#3548. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3547. 50 Years Later, Rocky's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Underdog Quote In Movie History

When we use the phrase "cinematic classic," there are some pretty universal movies that are likely to flash through one's mind. "The Godfather." "The Shawshank Redemption." "Psycho." "The Wizard of Oz." But undoubtedly amongst those all-time great titles is also "Rocky," the underdog story for the ages that made Sylvester Stallone a star.

The reception to "Rocky" upon release was a surprise for everyone involved. Not only was it a huge commercial hit, but it also went on to win Best Picture at the Oscars, with John G. Avildsen also winning Best Director. Not bad for a movie written and starring a guy nobody had really heard of before 1976.

Beyond the accolades though, 50 years later, "Rocky" is still so much more than a boxing movie. It's a remarkably crafted rags to riches story with a stellar performance by Stallone. It contains one of the best fights ever and the greatest training montage of all time. It also paved the way for a long-running, shockingly enduring franchise that led to some other great movies, including "Creed," which earned Stallone a Best Supporting Actor Oscar nomination decades after he first put on the gloves as Rocky Balboa.

For all of the movie's memorable moments and for all of its quotable lines, one quote sums up its underdog premise better than any other.

"All I wanna do is go the distance. Nobody's ever gone the distance with Creed, and if I can go that distance, you see, and that bell rings and I'm still standin', I'm gonna know for the first time in my life, see, that I weren't just another bum from the neighborhood." – Rocky Balboa

This quote really sums up the mission statement of the first "Rocky" movie in a nutshell. It's a true underdog story, right up until the end. It wasn't ever about him winning. This is a man who had nothing, felt like nothing, and was very unhappy with life as it existed. Given the opportunity, he made the very most of it and proved what he needed to prove to the world yes but, more importantly, to himself.

The ending of "Rocky" proves that he's not just another bum from the neighborhood. Win, lose, or draw, he went the distance with Apollo Creed, which made him a winner in a more meaningful way than winning any single boxing match. It's more about the journey than the destination. It's easy to be concerned about winning or achieving some goal that we believe might finally fix that hole deep inside of us but Rocky Balboa, with this quote, demonstrates a timeless understanding of what really matters.

Winning is great, but winning can take many forms. Rocky didn't defeat Creed but he won. He won a sense of purpose. He won a life he enjoyed. He won Adrian. He won in a far more meaningful way. This quote, once the movie's ending hits, rings loud and carries a lot of emotional weight.

"You're gonna eat lightnin' and you're gonna crap thunder!"

"My old man, he was never too smart. He says to me, 'You weren't born with much of a brain, so you better start using your body.' So I become a fighter."

"Forget about sports as a profession. Sports make ya grunt and smell. See, be a thinker, not a stinker."

"I been coming here for six years, and for six years ya been sticking it to me, and I wanna know how come!"

"Apollo Creed vs. the Italian Stallion. Sounds like a damn monster movie!"

#3546. ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.]

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

#3545. One Of GTA 6's Most Overlooked Mechanics Is Its Best

The release of Grand Theft Auto 6 has proven to be revolutionary in nearly every sense of the word. The new action-adventure title from Rockstar Games has excelled so much that GTA 6 has become the best-reviewed game of all time, finally surpassing 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. A lot of this comes from how well-designed all of the features it presents are. The several gameplay mechanics, the story, the attention to detail, the technical quality, and more make for a complete package that will provide players with over 100 hours of delightful gameplay.

In Screen Rant’s review of GTA 6, we mention that it “delivers on pretty much everything it promises,” while also taking a lesson from Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption 2, released in 2018. The new release has tons of different features to use and even uncover, such as a top-down zombie survival mini-game. Even though some of the new features are the ones taking the spotlight for themselves, there are also a few classic features that make a comeback. Among the several returning mechanics, there is one that is seriously overlooked in Rockstar’s new game.

Amidst all the chaos of Vice City and the larger state of Leonida, you can potentially find some serenity by pausing the action with the game’s photo mode. Since the last entry in the series, photo modes have evolved drastically and have become foundational to most AAA games nowadays. The photo mode in Final Fantasy 16, for example, allows for some pretty spectacular images, be they of moments of tranquility or intense combat. In GTA 6, it’s not all that different, apart from the fact that it’s an entirely different setting.

The new photo mode allows you to take some stunning pictures in GTA 6, be they centered around characters, locations, moments, and more. As you’d expect from a feature like this, you can change the camera angle, move it around, and adjust tons of other settings, such as lighting, poses, expressions, and much more, all to create the perfect opportunity for a click. This, combined with the cutting-edge ultra-realistic graphics the game has to offer, can make for some seriously breathtaking pictures. It’s all about experimenting and playing around with the photo mode.

Not every game with a photo mode provides the right tools or the right art direction to make moments worthy of being captured, but with a game like GTA 6, photo mode is nearly a game of its own. Depending on what you’re trying to capture, you’ll spend hours moving around Leonida and changing outfits in GTA 6 to get the perfect picture.

There’s no denying that Rockstar’s latest release is absolutely gorgeous. While the photo mode isn’t put in the spotlight as much as other fun features and additions to the franchise, such as the possibility of not being able to steal a vehicle or being mugged when using an ATM, the classic and ever-reliable photo mode is there, ready for you to use when you feel like capturing all the beauty Grand Theft Auto 6 has to offer.

#3543. Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026

““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a big improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

Effie Trinket, the character played by Elizabeth Banks in the original set of "Hunger Games" movies, is a larger-than-life, ridiculous, and flamboyant woman initially concerned with appearance above all else — even though her job is to beautify and briefly pamper impoverished children before they head to their deaths. It's hard to imagine this character, who appears in "The Hunger Games," "Catching Fire," and both parts of the adaptation of the book "Mockingjay," being played by anybody but Banks, yet the newest addition to the "Hunger Games" universe, the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," features a younger iteration of Effie. So, who brings her to life, and what role does Effie play in this prequel?

Suzanne Collins released the novel "Sunrise on the Reaping" in 2025, and before the book even hit shelves, a film adaptation (with the expanded title "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping") was in the works. Ultimately, Joseph Zada was cast as a young Haymitch Abernathy, the character made famous by Woody Harrelson alongside Banks in the first four "Hunger Games" movies. A ton of huge names, including Kieran Culkin, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, and Ralph Fiennes, went on to join the movie's cast from there, with Elle Fanning being recruited to fill Banks' sky-high pastel shoes and play Effie as well.

We see Effie in "Sunrise on the Reaping" as a fledgling stylist desperate to prove herself ... and not only does she end up styling Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes when a senior stylist falls through, but she provides emotional support to Haymitch before and after he wins the Games. But where have you seen Fanning before? Plenty of places.

If the last name "Fanning" just looks familiar from the outset, that's because Elle Fanning and her older sister Dakota Fanning have been performing since they were kids. In fact, the younger Fanning played a younger version of her sister while making her film debut in "I Am Sam" in 2001.

From there, Elle Fanning showed up in family-friendly fare like "Daddy Day Care" and "Because of Winn-Dixie" (as well as considerably more adult films like "Babel"), but the fact of the matter is that Fanning essentially grew up on-screen. Both Fanning sisters navigated their journeys from child stars to adult actors in pretty incredible ways, but we're talking about Elle Fanning here, and her career does stand on its own. After playing younger roles in "Super 8," "We Bought a Zoo," and "Maleficent," she moved into more firmly adult parts in the films "The Neon Demon," "20th Century Women," "The Beguiled," and "Mary Shelley," just to name a few.

Without question, Fanning's most visible big-screen appearances aside from "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" have recently come in "A Complete Unknown," "Predator: Badlands," and "Sentimental Value." In "A Complete Unknown," she plays Sylvie Russo, the girlfriend to Timothée Chalamet's Bob Dylan and a character who's loosely based on Dylan's real girlfriend Suze Rotolo. In "Predator: Badlands," Fanning plays the protagonist Thia and her evil twin sister Tessa and was able to use her own odd physicality for the role. As for "Sentimental Value," Joachim Trier's gorgeous family drama earned Fanning her first Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress at the 2026 ceremony.

Remarkably, Elle Fanning's small-screen career is just as robust as her big-screen one — and she's earned almost as much acclaim to boot. I personally remember seeing the younger Fanning as early as 2006 in the particularly depraved "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" episode "Cage" (fans of that show know exactly which one I'm talking about), but 2020 marked her big TV break with "The Great," a truly great — pun intended! — historical drama that casts Fanning as Catherine the Great. In this deliberately anachronistic, deeply funny, and exceptionally bawdy series created by "The Favourite" screenwriter Tony McNamara, Fanning gets to play the future Empress of Russia alongside a deliciously clownish Nicholas Hoult as her power-hungry and utterly twisted husband Emperor Peter III ... and earned her first Emmy nomination for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for her efforts.

Sadly, "The Great" ended in 2023 after only three seasons, although Fanning's next TV project, the crime drama miniseries "The Girl from Plainville," was well-received. In 2026, though, Fanning earned overwhelming acclaim and another Emmy nod for her lead role in "Margo's Got Money Troubles," a collaboration between A24 and Apple TV that proved to be one of the very best shows of the year. As a young single mother who launches an OnlyFans career as a colorful, coquettish alien to support her young son, Fanning is extraordinary as Margo, and it's clear that this ambitious and incredibly talented actor will keep racking up credits and accolades for years to come.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is currently in theaters.

#3541. Nintendo’s Long History with GTA Seems to Have Met Its End

Rockstar seems keen to bring all its games to Switch — except the biggest ones

Once upon a time, Rockstar Games regularly released Grand Theft Auto games on Nintendo consoles. Exclusive ones, even. Rockstar liked having its biggest franchise available on handhelds, which has always been Nintendo’s domain. The first two games in the series got cut-down Game Boy Color editions. In 2004, Grand Theft Auto Advance for the Game Boy Advance was a canonical prequel to GTA 3. In 2013, the massive DS audience tempted Rockstar to return with a GTA 4 spinoff, Chinatown Wars.

And since then... Nothing. Well, not quite nothing. Grand Theft Auto: The Trilogy — The Definitive Edition, which collects the "3D Universe" games GTA 3, Vice City, and San Andreas, is available on Switch, alongside every other platform known to humankind. The remasters are imperfect; the games are epoch-making. Their presence on the eShop proves that there's no inherent brand barrier, on either Rockstar's or Nintendo's side, to GTA existing on Switch.

It's a lot more difficult than you'd think

There's been much speculation about whether GTA 6 will come to Switch 2. I've no idea whether it's technically possible, but if the upcoming (and absolutely giant) Final Fantasy 7 Revelation can successfully fit and run on the thing, then maybe this can too. We have the Xbox Series S to thank for curbing the ambitions of AAA developers just enough, although Digital Foundry thinks GTA 6's CPU load may be just too high for Nintendo's console. But, to me, this isn't the pertinent question.

The question is: Where, exactly, is Grand Theft Auto 5?

GTA 5 began life on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, where it fit into a trim 17 GB. It seems like Switch should have been able to both fit it and run it, let alone Switch 2. The world-streaming demands of its huge map might be a challenge, but The Witcher 3 has been available for years. Why would Rockstar not have wanted the money-printing machine that is GTA Online accessible on 157 million Switches? I honestly don't know, although I wonder if Nintendo Switch Online's rather feeble feature set and notorious technical hiccups on the original console were an issue. Switch 2 seems better-suited.

The strange thing is that Rockstar is far from allergic to publishing on Nintendo, and seems to see the value of putting its other franchises there. Table Tennis, Bully, and Manhunt 2 were all released on Wii. Even the games made in GTA's cinematic image, and for its older audience, are on Switch: L.A Noire and Red Dead Redemption. Red Dead received a Switch 2 Edition as recently as December. And yet Rockstar's biggest game is still AWOL.

Nintendo's consoles are never going to be a priority for Rockstar. The audience, which has certainly garnered the reputation of being more family-oriented than PlayStation and Xbox, is not in their sweet spot. Nevertheless, it seems to be worth the studio's while to port its games eventually — except in GTA's case. We can only guess at why. Rockstar is — with the exception of the Trilogy release — very protective of the technical quality and integrity of its games. Maybe Rockstar simply never got GTA 5 or GTA Online running on Switch to its satisfaction. Maybe it's experimenting with Switch 2 right now. But I wouldn't hold your breath. Rockstar used to bend its franchises into new shapes to fit onto new platforms. Now it looks for platforms that can accommodate its vision. For now, that's not Nintendo.

Does it matter? The Switch 2 will never be the best place to play GTA 6; no other platform will ever have a Mario or Zelda game. That's a more than fair trade. Jockeying for dominion over big third-party franchises is good sport for fanboys, but does anybody honestly care that they can play Call of Duty on Switch 2 now? The Nintendo difference is just that: difference. We can let them have this one.

It's not a new release by any means, but I feel mysteriously compelled to recommend a driving game with an open-world city map this week, and you can hardly do better than this clean remaster of Criterion's arcade racing classic.

There are no exact replicas, but Fuse's debut has some fascinating predecessors

If you've got jetskis on the mind — maybe due to Switch Sports Resort? I can't think of any other reason — you could do worse than revisit this charming relic from a time when a simple racing game with a unique gimmick and slick technology was a viable proposition. The GameCube's Blue Storm is the one you really want, but that's not on Classics yet.

Don't know why I'm feeling in the mood for summery synthwave vibes right now, but I am, and this immaculate track from Pilotwings Resort is really hitting the spot. (You can find the full playlist of Switchboard picks here.)

#3540. 5 Actors Who Should Play Q In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

The next era of the "James Bond" movie franchise is upon us. After years of waiting and endless speculation, Robert Pattinson is officially the next Bond and is replacing Daniel Craig. The Craig era firmly and definitively came to an end in 2021 with "No Time to Die." Now? The former "Twilight" and current "The Batman" star gets to put his stamp on 007. But what about his supporting cast?

Making a new "Bond" film doesn't just mean casting a new MI6 agent. It means filling out some other key roles, and that includes Q, aka the quartermaster and head of Q Branch at MI6. This is historically the individual who outfits Bond with his various gadgets and field equipment for his missions. Ben Whishaw made his debut as Q in "Skyfall" during the Craig era, serving as one of only a small handful of actors to take on that responsibility.

The character made a brief appearance in "Dr. No" as "Major Boothroyd" played by Peter Burton, but for the lion's share of this franchise's existence, it was the late, great Desmond Llewelyn who played Q, with his tenure extending all the way from "From Russia with Love" to "The World is Not Enough." That was one heck of a run. Now, though, it's time for the next chapter.

So, who will suit up as Q for "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve and outfit Pattinson's Bond for his next mission? We're going to go over five actors who should be considered for the role, for various reasons. Let's get into it.

This may seem too obvious and perhaps even painful for the actor involved, but it also makes sense. Robert Pattinson's "James Bond" casting continued an unfortunate trend for Nicholas Hoult as he's always the bridesmaid, never the bride. He was the runner up for Batman in "The Batman" and the runner up for Superman in "Superman." Now? He was one of the finalists for Bond before Pattinson nabbed the role. It's been a rough run for the actor.

Be that as it may, much in the same way that missing out on Superman made him a damn fine Lex Luthor, he could be a very good Q in Denis Villeneuve's currently untitled "Bond" movie. For one, it's pretty darn easy to picture Hoult as a smart guy in a lab coat. His work as Beast in the "X-Men" films proved that well enough, and he's only become a better actor in the years since joining that franchise, so there's no question he could pull it off.

More importantly, Bond and Q have always had something of a playfully contentious relationship in the movies. "Pay attention, 007!" and all that jazz. Hoult might have a little bit of playful bitterness and/or jealousy to work with when it comes to Pattinson as Bond. That could provide a lot of on-screen fuel and chemistry for the dynamic between these two.

Now, would Hoult want to settle for Q after missing out on the big prize? That's unclear, but if he's open to it, this could be a fun option.

Samantha Morton is an actor who has been doing it at a very high level for a very long time, yet she remains somewhat unappreciated. Now, though, Morton has made herself more familiar to audiences as Circe in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," delivering a scene-stealing performance in a movie filled with A-listers who all brought their A game. That list of actors just so happens to include Robert Pattinson. So, even though the pair didn't share any screen time, their reunion here would be a nice story in and of itself.

But more than that, Morton is a wildly flexible performer of immense talent. From sci-fi movies like "Minority Report" to hit TV shows such as "The Walking Dead," she's been everywhere and done it all. Morton is often a pretty serious actor, too, and she could bring a stern quality to Q. At the same time, the role would allow her to loosen up a bit, which would undoubtedly be fun to see from an artist of her caliber.

Morton will also be in her 50s by the time filming on the next "James Bond" movie truly gets underway, so her age provides her with a believable wisdom that she could impart onto Pattinson's Bond. Indeed, there's something about the notion of a quartermaster in these movies that benefits from someone who feels like they lived a life before being relegated to Q Branch. It's been missing ever since Desmond Llewelyn passed, and Morton could bring it back with her own, unique twist.

If Denis Villeneuve and the brass at Amazon want to use the new Q for some dry comedic relief, as opposed to going the more serious route, it's hard to imagine a better fit for the role than Richard Ayoade. One of the most consistently funny British comedians of the current generation, it's almost too easy to picture him in a lab coat giving Robert Pattinson's 007 the business before he heads out on a mission.

Ayoade has a very distinct, very British, and at times delightfully dry sense of humor. It's the sort of trait that's easy to picture someone with Q's job having. Ayoade is also a damn fine writer and director, so he could be an asset to the production overall. Heck, NBC tried to remake "The IT Crowd" more than once and failed more than once, as Ayoade and the distinctive sense of humor he brought to that show are quite difficult to pull off.

This particular casting choice relies an awful lot on the direction of this new iteration of the franchise. Villeneuve is a pretty serious storyteller and, for that reason, Ayoade might be a long shot. That's not to say that he couldn't turn in a dramatic performance, but the benefit of casting him is foremost comedic relief. If Villeneuve strikes a balance between humor and grit, recalling something closer to "GoldenEye" than "Casino Royale," then it's easier to envision.

Basically, if the shoe fits, Ayoade feels like a slam dunk casting choice.

If the idea was just, "Let's find the very best actor we can and offer her the role of Q in this movie," then it would be tough to do better than Emma Thompson. These things are subjective, but she's a two-time Oscar winner and a five-time Oscar nominee who has been one of the best actors working pretty much for as long as we've known her name. If she says yes, you say thank you.

At first glance, it might make more sense to have Thompson play M rather than Q. And look, if Denis Villeneuve offered her the role of M, I'd happily get behind it. That said, some of Thompson's best work is on the more playful side, be it her turn in Hugh Jackman's must-watch murder mystery "The Sheep Detectives" or the criminally under-seen "Stranger Than Fiction." Yes, she's about as good as it gets when she puts on her serious hat in movies like "The Remains of the Day" as well. We can't forget that.

Q could give her an opportunity to have some fun while flexing every facet of her acting chops. A director like Villeneuve has a knack for getting the most out of great actors, even if it's in a smaller role. See: Dave Bautista in "Dune." As such, letting an actor as good as Thompson eat up the scenery in a "James Bond" movie as Q would be an asset to this new iteration of the franchise.

Would Thompson be interested in doing such a thing? Would she rather play a Bond villain? It's tough to say, but if this came up, and Thompsan entertained saying yes, that would pretty much be the end of the discussion. Finding a "better" actor is going to be tough.

Last, but certainly not least, we come to the most obvious of the bunch, if not the most realistic in this particular scenario. Ben Whishaw made his entry into the franchise during the Daniel Craig era. "Skyfall" remains the biggest "James Bond" movie ever, which just so happens to be the first time audiences saw Whishaw as Q. He remained on board for the rest of the Craig era, including "Spectre" and "No Time to Die." So, why not just have him stay on board for the Robert Pattinson era?

In most cases in modern franchise filmmaking, reboot means total reset. However, the "James Bond" movies aren't like any other property. Desmond Llewelyn was the quartermaster for every single Bond save for Craig. Judi Dench was the M for both Pierce Brosnan and Craig. You get the idea. This film series has always played it a little more fast and loose with continuity in that way. Granted, Amazon is now in the driver's seat, and it seems to be changing things up already. Specifically, Pattinson's Bond casting broke a 60-year-old 007 tradition, as he's the biggest established movie star to ever take on the part.

For that reason, it seems far more likely that Denis Villeneuve and Amazon will move forth with a total reboot. However, if they decide to keep some level of tradition alive, bringing Whishaw back wouldn't be a bad call. He's even a little older now, which might allow him to bring something a bit different to the role this time around. There's no denying that he had something unique to offer.

Again, this may not be the most realistic choice, but in many ways, it's the most logical one.

The new "James Bond" movie doesn't have a release date yet, so stay tuned.

#3539. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3538. ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.]

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.)

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

#3537. Peter Jackson's The Lord Of The Rings Failed One Of Tolkien's Most Dangerous Villains

Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings is an absolute masterpiece, a loving tribute to J.R.R. Tolkien's epic novels. They're not perfect, of course; despite their phenomenal length, they cut a huge number of scenes and plot elements. Tom Bombadil is missing, for example, while the final battle against Saruman at the Shire is completely absent. That particular cut has proven deeply controversial, with fans still debating it today.

Oddly, though, that's part of a wider mistake made in The Lord of the Rings. In the books, that Shire battle is the culmination of a story that played out very differently to Tolkien's movies. And, importantly, it means the Peter Jackson films actually failed one specific character—one of Tolkien's most complex villains.

Played by Brad Dourif, Grima Wormtongue was a manipulative adviser to King Théoden. In the books, he's a subtle schemer who'd been given his nickname by his political enemies, who'd learned to fear his Machiavellian cunning. Wormtongue was cruel and ambitious, a servant of Saruman who had proven far more successful than his master anticipated. He'd subtly undermined Théoden's reign, bringing the kingdom of Rohan to the brink of destruction.

The book version of Grima Wormtongue doesn't achieve this through magic. Instead, he's simply the consumate politician, proof that you don't need physical power or sorcerous ability to be a dangerous villain. He reinforced this through the use of poisons, leaving his opponents under his thrall. He may have supposedly been an adviser, but the ambitious Grima Wormtongue had essentially taken over the entire kingdom before he was exposed and defeated by Gandalf the White.

Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings took a different approach, though. Here, the scene where Gandalf frees Théoden makes it abundantly clear he was enchanted; he has lost all strength and vitality because he is ensorcelled, unable to exercise free will. More to the point, when Gandalf breaks the spell, it isn't Wormtongue who is sent flying. No, Saruman himself is shocked as his power is broken, because he is the one who has really taken control of Rohan.

The difference is an important one. In Tolkien's books, Grima Wormtongue has a power all of his own, one not even Saruman possesses; he's still a tool, but one who is dangerous enough to operate independently, and who doesn't need the wizard's magic of Saruman to make him more dangerous. In contrast, in the films, he is essentially a channel; Saruman pours his magic through him, using Grime as a way to get to King Théoden. Wormtongue is, oddly, so much more dangerous.

Looking back, I can't help feeling Peter Jackson largely failed Grima Wormtongue. He turned Grima into something so much less than Tolkien intended, making him nothing more than a pawn (albeit one who eventually strikes back). Even his final scenes were rewritten, because Grima's compressed plotline was supposed to end at the Shire. It's one of the few missteps in Jackson's The Lord of the Rings.

#3536. Why Sylvester Stallone's Father In I Play Rocky Looks So Familiar

Peter Farrelly's biopic "I Play Rocky" tells the story of a young Sylvester Stallone (Anthony Ippolito) as he rises through his early, sketchy acting career, eventually coming to write and star in 1976's "Rocky," itself one of the best sports movies ever made. The film doesn't sugarcoat Stallone's early struggles, including his run-down apartment, his inability to land good roles as a young actor going by the name of Mike (leading him to work on an adult feature), and the fact that, at one point, he had to sleep on the street.

It also depicts the verbal abuse that he suffered at the hands of his domineering father, Frank Sr, who runs a barbershop and is hardly encouraging. When Stallone relates his acting dreams, Frank tells his son that he isn't handsome enough to be a movie star. Ouch, dad.

Frank is played by Matt Dillon, who exploded onto the cinematic scene in 1979 thanks to his role in Jonathan Kaplan's "Over the Edge," a film so beloved that it inspired both Richard Linklater and Kurt Cobain. Dillon rose to prominence shortly after that, appearing in movies like "Little Darlings," "Liar's Moon," and Francis Ford Coppola's S.E. Hinton adaptations "The Outsiders" and "Rumble Fish."

Indeed, for a spell during the 1980s, Dillon was a teen heartthrob, and his intense performance style and tenacity dictated a steady stream of high-profile work as he got older. That includes his role in Gun Van Sant's 1989 picture "Drugstore Cowboy" (which caused quite a stir) and his turn in Cameron Crowe's 1992 movie "Singles" (one of the 1990s' defining films). From there, he collaborated with Van Sant again when he played a pushy husband in 1995's "To Die For" and had a key role in Frank Oz's mainstream 1997 queer comedy "In & Out.

Listing all of Matt Dillon's credits here would take up too much space. Just know that he has been a creative force in Hollywood for, gosh, almost 50 years, and has constantly teamed up with prominent directors, among them Garry Marshall, Arthur Penn, Allison Anders, Lars Von Trier, and Wes Anderson. His role as  Frank Stallone Sr. in "I Play Rocky" isn't even the first time Dillon has played a real person. In fact, he previously played Marlon Brando in the Maria Schneider biopic "Being Maria" and Henri Chinaski, Charles Bukowski's literary alter ego, in the 2005 film "Factotum."

"I Play Rocky" itself marks the second time Dillon has worked with Peter Farrelly, as he also appeared in the Farrelly Bros.' 1998 ultra-hit comedy "There's Something About Mary," playing the toothsome character of Pat. That same year, he played a sleazy, double-crossing teacher in the thriller "Wild Things" and thereafter worked on everything from Disney films ("Herbie: Fully Loaded") to the notorious Best Picture Oscar-winning "Crash," whose own director, Paul Haggis, later admitted didn't deserve to be crowned Best Picture. Nevertheless, Dillon is excellent in it.

Even now, Dillon shows no signs of slowing down. And while he specializes in playing tough guys and aggressive heavies, he's quite capable of other things, with "Drugstore Cowboy" displaying his range with what, for my money, is his best performance. But then, there are so many to choose from. He does a good job as an oppressive father figure in the syrupy but highly watchable "I Play Rocky," too, embodying a hard-working barber who may love his son but doesn't think much of him. It's a solid, dark turn for a longtime, hardworking actor.

#3535. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3534. 'The Odyssey' Cast Debunks a Major Misconception About Working with Christopher Nolan

Matt Damon, Himesh Patel, and Emma Thomas reveal Nolan's unexpected sense of humor and what he's really like on set.

Christopher Nolan doesn't exactly have a reputation for being the life of the party. The Oscar-winning director is known for meticulously constructed films, complicated narratives, and productions that demand an extraordinary amount of preparation. His movies routinely deal with weighty subjects, whether it's the nature of time, the consequences of scientific discovery, or humanity's place in the universe. Not exactly the kind of material that screams laugh riot.

But according to the cast and crew of The Odyssey, there's another side to Nolan that audiences might not expect. Behind the intense focus and demanding production schedules is a filmmaker with a sharp sense of humor who genuinely loves being on a movie set.

Speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, several members of the production shared what might surprise audiences about working with Nolan. Their answers revealed a director who enjoys a good joke, even if he isn't about to let it interfere with making a movie.

Himesh Patel, who plays Eurylochus, the second-in-command to Matt Damon's Odysseus, recalled a production that wasn't nearly as solemn as Nolan's reputation might suggest. According to Patel, Nolan's humor has a distinctly British quality.

"He's got a cutting sense of humor," Patel says. "It's that British sense of humor that can just be very sardonic. But I've always found it funny."

That might surprise viewers who associate Nolan primarily with the intense atmosphere of films like Oppenheimer, Interstellar, and The Dark Knight. But Patel suggested that Nolan's enjoyment of filmmaking is just as evident as his attention to detail.

"There is a lot of fun because I think ultimately he takes the work seriously," Patel explains. "The bar is set very high. Everyone's there to work hard and fulfill the vision that we're there to fulfill. But he's also like a kid living his dreams."

Patel suggested that Nolan is keenly aware of how fortunate he is to be making movies, and that enthusiasm extends to his willingness to get directly involved in the process.

"That's why he likes to get his hands dirty. He likes to be a part of it, 'cause it's fun," Patel says. That doesn't mean the work is easy. Patel described a demanding production where the cast and crew could find themselves physically exhausted after a take. But those moments could also be surprisingly entertaining.

"The amount of times that we'd get a take and Matt [Damon] would be laughing and Chris would be finding it really funny, and we'd be sort of out of breath and exhausted," Patel recalls. "But it's part of the fun."

Few people have a better understanding of Nolan's personality than Emma Thomas, his wife and longtime producing partner. Thomas has worked alongside Nolan throughout his filmmaking career, helping bring his ambitious projects to the screen. When asked what audiences might be surprised to learn about him, she pointed to his sense of humor.

"He's very funny. People always think that's a crazy thing," Thomas tells Polygon. "He's quite lighthearted on set."

Thomas acknowledged that Nolan isn't always joking around. There are moments when the demands of directing require complete seriousness. She suggested that the place where he seems most comfortable is also the place where he's doing some of his most demanding work.

"There's often times where he has to be dead serious to get the job done, but a movie set is his happy place," Thomas explains. "He is never happier than when he's standing on a movie set."

It's an interesting contrast with the public image of a director whose work often explores serious subjects. For Thomas, though, Nolan's enjoyment of filmmaking is something she witnesses firsthand.

Matt Damon offered a slightly different perspective on Nolan's humor. Yes, the director enjoys a good joke, but there's a limit to how much time he's willing to spend laughing when there's a movie to make.

"I think people know how hard he pushes himself and everybody around him, in a good way," Damon tells Polygon. "But I think he's got a great sense of humor."

Damon suggested that Nolan's reluctance to let the joking go too far has less to do with being overly serious and more to do with maintaining the production's momentum.

"He doesn't love to laugh because I think if you start laughing too much, it feels like you're not getting the work done," Damon explains. "But he does love a laugh."

That distinction seems to capture Nolan's approach to directing. Humor is welcome, provided it doesn't bring the production to a standstill.

"He won't let anyone get carried away," Damon says. "The momentum is never gonna stop because he is a momentum-driven director."

Special effects supervisor Scott Fisher described a similar atmosphere around the camera, where Nolan works closely with a relatively small group that includes cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, and camera assistants. Fisher said there's often a little ribbing and joking among the group throughout the day.

"He's got a really good sense of humor, but he doesn't like to show too much," Fisher tells Polygon.

#3533. What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”

#3532. Slow Horses Star Jack Lowden's Breakout Role Came In A Christopher Nolan Movie

"Slow Horses" is the best spy show on TV for many reasons, one of which is seeing veteran star and British national treasure Gary Oldman sharing scenes with relative newcomers, especially River Cartwright actor Jack Lowden. But while the Scottish star seemed to come out of nowhere when Apple TV's spy series debuted in 2020, he's actually been working since the early 2010s. By 2016, he'd landed a lead role in the BBCs "War & Peace" miniseries, which was a major step in his career. The following year, however, was arguably even more significant for Lowden as he not only played Morrissey in the unauthorized biopic "England is Mine," he had a significant part in Christopher Nolan's "Dunkirk."

Nolan made yet another great film with "Dunkirk." It depicts the evacuation of thousands of Allied troops from the titular French region during the six-week Battle of France in 1940. But in true Nolan style, we get a non-linear narrative and multiple perspectives on the legendary events that unfolded on the French coast. The writer/director follows two young soldiers on land named Tommy (Fionn Whitehead) and Gibson (Aneurin Barnard), civilian sailor Mr Dawson (Mark Rylance) and his son Peter Dawson (Tom Glynn-Carney), and two fighter pilots named Farrier (Tom Hardy) and Collins (Lowden).

The various characters' harrowing journeys intersect as Nolan's retelling of the historic event goes on. Thankfully, Lowden isn't relegated to wearing an oxygen mask in a cockpit for the entire film, and is given quite a bit to do despite the expansive ensemble. One of his scenes in particular represents one of the film's most gripping moments. But Lowden is also able to showcase his talents in smaller moments as a shellshocked pilot left reeling from his experience in the skies over the English Channel.

Like all Christopher Nolan movies, most of the events in "Dunkirk" are captured in-camera using real props and vehicles. That lends the film an authenticity which adds so much to the experience. When Collins' plane goes down, for instance, you feel the thud as it hits the water. The following scene, wherein his cockpit fills with water, feels similarly visceral, bringing you into the experience and heightening the sense of panic. It's incredibly well done and beautifully shot by cinematographer and frequent Nolan collaborator Hoyte van Hoytema.

But there's more to "Dunkirk" than visceral action sequences. Every aspect of the film comes together to create an unforgettable whole, and the performances are a big part of that. Nolan deliberately keeps dialogue to a minimum — a blessing for those who find his writing to be a tad overwrought at times — leaving the cast with the challenge of rendering the emotion through their reactions and expressions. Everyone, Jack Lowden included, delivers.

Not that that should be a surprise to "Slow Horses" fans. The actor, who's said to be one of five finalists to become the new James Bond, has been brilliant as River Cartwright, never allowing his humanistic portrayal of the frustrated sleuth to be overshadowed by his esteemed co-star's unforgettable performance as Jackson Lamb. Lowden fans, along with everyone else yet to see "Dunkirk," should definitely watch Nolan's war epic.

#3531. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes.
