#3507. 9 Years Ago, Jon Bernthal Teamed With Taylor Sheridan to Deliver His Most Devastating Performance

Jon Bernthal is known for his gun-toting, intense characters, but one of his best depictions of masculinity was only for a few scenes of screen time in Taylor Sheridan’s masterpiece, Wind River. After writing Sicario and Hell or High Water, Sheridan directed his own feature film that takes on yet another strictly American issue. The neo-Western takes place on the titular Indian Reservation, following the sudden death of a young Indigenous woman, Natalie (Kelsey Asbille). Statistics about crimes against this demographic do not exist, which is the stark point Wind River makes.

As local hunter Cory Lambert (Jeremy Renner) and FBI Agent Jane Banner (Elizabeth Olsen) set out to solve the murder, they explore the systemic oppression against Indigenous people, particularly the female demographic. Natalie is just one of many women on Reservations who are harmed and ignored in America. Bernthal also joins the cast in a surprise role that hammers home this idea in one of his most devastating performances.

Wind River is a scathing view of the plight of Indian Reservations and how the community is treated by the government. Cory is particularly motivated by Natalie’s death because she was best friends with his daughter, Emily, who also died under similar circumstances. Even as Jane gets involved in the investigation, she is railroaded by the law, causing even more frustration about how a community is so neglected by the country they live in.

Cory and Jane take it upon themselves to go rogue and follow the clues that at first seem to lead to Natalie’s white, older boyfriend. They discover she was dating Matt Rayburn (Jon Bernthal), a security agent at a local oil drilling site, and suspect him of killing her. The truth is much more harrowing when they also find Matt’s body dumped in the cold.

Bernthal appears briefly in a heartbreaking flashback that drives the central thesis of Wind River home. Natalie and Matt genuinely love each other, a fact that is palpable in the scene. Natalie visits him at his trailer, but their quiet moment of affection is disrupted by drunk men who work at the site. They invade the communal area of the trailer before alcohol and loneliness cause them to attack Natalie.

Natalie is assaulted by them as Matt tries to protect her. He sacrifices his own life so that Natalie can run barefoot in the snow to get away from her assailants. For his trouble – and for simply loving a girl – he is beaten to death and thrown away like garbage. Casting Bernthal may have been a clever way of playing against the type of his typically darker characters.

When he first appears on-screen, there is a moment of dread as it seems for a moment that he could be the murderer. Instead, Matt brightens when he sees Natalie, exuding pure joy at seeing the person he loves. Matt is the only decent man at the oil site, laying down his life so he can save his girlfriend. This is even more tragic because his efforts are for naught.

Natalie runs six miles barefoot in the snow to escape, but her trauma and the cold lead to her freezing to death in the night. While the men did not technically kill her, they are 100 percent responsible for her death. Bernthal is an underrated part of this complex narrative that showed the heights the actor was capable of. In only one scene, Bernthal completely steals the show in his best and most devastating performance.

#3506. 10 Shows Like 'Youth' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3505. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

#3504. Doomsday's Missing Avenger Snub Is Even Worse After Scarlet Witch's Return

While a lot of MCU fans might have been waiting for this to happen for a long time, Scarlet Witch's return from the dead for Avengers: Doomsday is still one of the biggest swings the franchise has taken in years. After her sacrifice at Mount Wundagore at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, bringing Wanda Maximoff back into the fold, and shockingly as a recruit of Doctor Doom, changes everything for the upcoming Avengers crossover. It also means we're going to see even more trauma piled onto an already tragic storyline, as Wanda will once again potentially be involved in major deaths.

Despite speculation of her return, at some point her late addition to the Avengers: Doomsday cast was genuinely a surprise, especially given how tightly Marvel has guarded the movie's biggest secrets. We may be in for more, as the Russo brothers have openly teased that the roster probably still isn't finished and there will be more surprises to come, even if they're only revealed when Doomsday is released.

There are some fairly major characters still missing from Avengers: Doomsday who fans expect to see: Captain Marvel being one of them, Deadpool and Wolverine, and even Spider-Man as a possibly wishful further inclusion, while the complete absence of the entire Young Avengers cast is just confusing at this point. With several heavy hitters still notably absent from the officially confirmed lineup, it feels like more characters will definitely turn up before the multiverse starts collapsing. But with Scarlet Witch back in play, one missing Avenger in particular stands out above the rest as a glaring omission.

Despite some rumours of his involvement, Clint Barton being left out of the Avengers: Doomsday cast so far has already been a bit of a tough pill to swallow for fans of the original Avengers. With the narrative suggesting that Doomsday and Secret Wars may be the farewell for the remaining original Avengers, him being snubbed doesn't really make sense. Now that Scarlet Witch is officially returning as one of Doctor Doom's personal weapons, Hawkeye's lack of involvement also means there's a big gap in the story.

Going back to Wanda's full debut in Avengers: Age of Ultron, she and Clint shared a genuine bond almost immediately, as he was positioned as the somewhat unwilling handler of the future Scarlet Witch and her brother, Quicksilver. He was positioned as the veteran hero who looked after them during the Sokovian firefight with Ultron and effectively stepped in as a surrogate father, especially after Pietro died. He also stood by her during the fallout of Captain America: Civil War and rescued her from isolation when the Avengers' fear locked her up.

From Wanda's point of view, assuming she still believes Vision is gone forever and her kids with him, Clint is arguably the most significant personal connection she has left in the world. Removing him from the equation robs Doomsday of an excellent emotional moment. Just imagine the gut punch of Clint stepping onto the battlefield to face Doctor Doom's forces and seeing a corrupted Wanda standing across the lines alongside Victor, without Hawkeye there to confront her or at least for an added reaction to what she has probably become. The movie loses a crucial human element that would ground one of its biggest in-universe shocks.

And it isn't just Clint Barton who was a glaring omission. Now that we know that Scarlet Witch is back, having Vision sit on the sidelines is now almost unthinkable too, especially after the events of VisionQuest's ending, thanks to a solo season.

White Vision has effectively had a total reset, with all of his original memories restored, and he has been reunited with both of his sons. He remembers Wanda, the life they built together, and the grief that drove Wanda towards the Darkhold in the first place. Leaving him out of Doomsday may be necessary at first to keep Wanda on Doom's side, but it makes zero narrative sense for them not to come back together.

Bringing both Hawkeye and Vision back into the fold also isn't just about ticking boxes for who's missing in Doomsday. It's about giving Scarlet Witch a path back to genuine redemption. Clint can be an advocate for her when some of the other heroes may defer back to suspecting that she's been evil all along, while Vision represents the future that she thought she'd lost. If Doom is weaponizing her trauma and isolation to use her as a weapon to his own ends, having Vision (ideally alongside both Billy and Tommy) be the one to break through his hold and pull her back from the brink is the best way to complete her redemption arc.

She cannot die again, and she needs and deserves this happy ending. Avengers: Doomsday already has enough spectacle; it needs this smaller, quieter moment of personal emotion to resolve one of the most complex and compelling story arcs in the entire franchise.

Avengers: Doomsday is scheduled to release worldwide on December 18.

#3503. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3500. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

#3499. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.

This year, I made my first visit to Scandinavia for a behind-the-scenes tour of the cutting-edge MIPS helmet test facility in Stockholm, Sweden. I also ran my first 5K while testing out new Garmin watches in Durham, North Carolina. And I was fortunate enough to cover several international trade shows for TG, including Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, CES in Las Vegas, and IFA in Berlin.

To keep spirits high during even the most head-scratching travel kerfuffles, I turned to my time-tested toolkit of accessories that make even 13+ hour flights (and the days that follow), all-day car rides, epic train delays, etc. feel like the smallest of potatoes.

This list (below) includes everything from $12 inflatable seat cushions that will save your butt to remarkably versatile and durable luggage; also, the best cheap (and splurge-worthy) entertainment devices and even my favorite fancy-yet-thrifty travel slippers. Happy trails!

Looking for more gift inspiration? Check out our guide to the best holiday gifts.

Picture this: You land in a new country, excited to start exploring. You check into your hotel and go to juice your phone up, but oh no! You've forgotten your AC plug adapter. Or worse, you brought the wrong one (guilty). Avoid this reality from ever happening with Epicka's sturdy-built universal adapter. It works with the four most common outlet types, which translates to compatibility in 150+ countries.

Never misplace your keys, car, smartphone, wallet, or luggage again with one of these little round trackers. Sold individually or in four-packs, they offer peace of mind for those on the move, especially when checked bags and short connections are part of the itinerary. Learn more in our Apple AirTag 2 review.

When you're on the go, you can't count on having a great entertainment option. Bring it with you with the GT Max. It pairs built-in 3DoF spatial tracking with a 59° field of view — the largest in the industry. Dual-chip Zone 360 silicon pins a virtual screen of up to 307 inches in place without your device needing to process it and without a companion app to set up. A single USB-C cable connects it to your PC, phone or major console with 120Hz Micro-OLED panels and quad speakers co-tuned by Bang & Olufsen.

The latest generation Apple Watch SE 3 is a fabulous travel companion and the best budget Apple Watch in 2026. It even comes in an LTE version for those who prefer to leave their smartphone back at the hotel while they explore.

The Apple Watch Series 12, one of the best smartwatches in 2026, just hit its lowest price ever ahead of the 2026 holiday season. Moreover, compared to the Series 11, it boasts improved heart rate tracking accuracy, impressive new health and safety tools, and support for some exclusive AI features.

The Google Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best full-featured smartwatches of 2026 for battery life and onboard safety tools. For instance, no other brand has Google's Loss Pulse Detection or Breathing Emergency Detection, which can automatically call for help in an emergency.

The Fitbit Edge replaces 2023's popular Fitbit Charge 6. Easily the most well-rounded and best fitness tracker for most people in 2026, It's a wearable I'll likely be recommending well into the foreseeable future.

The Fitbit Air isn't as advanced as the Fitbit Edge. It also lacks a screen or any buttons, but it's my favorite fitness tracker for anyone who hates wearing a fitness tracker. Ridiculously lightweight and discreet, it looks more like a bracelet than a piece of flashy tech... and that's the point.

The Camp Snap 2 is an affordable, retro-tastic, screen-free digital camera with smartphone-like performance and a playful, pocket-friendly design. This makes it a great choice for kids and casual adult photographers alike.

The Fujifilm Instax Mini 41 is a stylish and compact instant camera that makes use of the brand's smallest (and most affordable) Instax Mini format. Dead-simple to operate with no shortage of retro charm, the Mini 41 is a great road trip companion. Find out more in our Fujifilm Instax Mini 41 review.

This $99 point-and-shoot 35mm film camera punches well above its price point in terms of image quality. Think of it like a disposable camera, but built to last. Powered by a single AA battery, this little wonder accepts any type of 35mm film stock.

In our Nikon Z5 II review, we called it "an unbeatable value for the money" thanks to brilliant imaging performance and exceptionally well-laid-out controls, a bright and crisp electronic viewfinder, and rock-solid autofocus performance. Oh, and it's no slouch at shooting video, either. No wonder we named the Nikon Z5 II digital camera the best camera for most people in 2026.

I tested out the new Nocs Field Issue Binoculars while hiking to the top of one of the infamous peaks shown in the TV classic, "Twin Peaks." Needless to say, these lightweight, impact-resistant, water-sealed optics left me stunned when I took a gander through them from the top.

Theragun's most compact massage gun doesn't skimp on the power. With three intensities to choose from and a low-profile design, this little device is the ultimate travel and adventure companion, especially after an eight-hour flight in coach. By the way, it's TSA-friendly, too.

Combine this super-soft sleeping mask with a good pair of noise-canceling headphones, like the Bose QuietComforts below, for a relaxing in-flight experience, even in the middle seat. The Mavogel Eye Mask provides complete darkness and is adjustable to fit any head size. They also come with a lovely little travel pouch.

A decent inflatable neck pillow just may be the ultimate travel hack. This one is just $9 and has a soft, machine-washable cover. Inflation takes just a couple of breaths into the one-way air valve. And when deflated, the Keemall can be packed into a small carrying case for easy stowage.

This $12 inflatable cushion also takes up almost no space in your bag and requires only two or three full breaths to inflate. I just brought one along on a flight from Seattle, Washington, to Florence, Italy (~13 hours) and back, and was seriously shocked by how much more comfortable it made my economy seat.

Keep important items, like sunglasses, hand sanitizer, charging cables, etc., close at hand with this stylish and lightweight hip pack. The Terravia Mini wears comfortably around the waist or across the body and stows easily in a carry-on until you're ready to board.

For my hardcore coffee drinkers out there, I swear by this affordable yet reliable travel mug. Whether hitting the airport or the freeway, it comes along, keeping bevs toasty. Most importantly, it doesn't leak, and the lid stays closed. Plus, it's dishwasher-friendly.

Beyond being well-rested, staying hydrated is one of the keys to beating Jet Lag. To do that, you need a good refillable vessel. The Hydro Flask is our favorite water bottle for travel because of its thin, attractive design and outstanding insulation that keeps bevs cold for 24 hours or more. It also comes in an array of snazzy colors.

This one is for anyone who has ever wanted to watch an in-flight movie with their seatmate without having to sync up two screens. The AirFly Pro 2 from Twelve South plugs into a standard 3.5mm audio jack and wirelessly transmits audio to up to two Bluetooth-enabled headphones. How romantic.

I spend more of my waking hours rocking a pair of Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 headphones than I'd like to admit. As someone who's quite easily distracted and/or irked by distracting noises, these heavenly ear cans are one of the best investments I've ever made. They also happen to be the best overall noise-canceling headphones of 2026.

If you're looking for a more affordable alternative to the Bose above, I've got you covered. For less than $100, the JLab JBuds Lux ANC pack a mighty punch, with impressive sound quality and battery life for the price.

Want the best noise-cancelling earbuds money can buy? Say no more. The latest-generation Bose QuietComforts will isolate you in a tranquil zone of peace and quiet. Audio quality is also excellent, which is perhaps why we called them the new standard for noise cancellation in our Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds review.

For some affordable ear candy, check out these JLab Go Pods ANC wireless earbuds. For around $25, they provide solid audio quality in a petite and stylish package. They also boast decent battery life and a durable design, which is why we selected them as our best value wireless earbuds in 2026.

This oddly-named backpack is full of secret compartments and features, including an oversized weather-resistant roll-top for expanding storage and a hideaway water bottle pocket. The main area is also highly configurable, with plenty of space for gadgets and gear — there are even separate sections for a laptop and a tablet. Oh, and it fits nicely under the seat in front.

Far cheaper than the Wandrd backpack above, this sub-$100 Topo Designs backpack is ultra-stylish and functional. While there aren't quite as many secret compartments as on the Prvke, the Rover Pack Classic offers ample space in a lightweight and weather-resistant package that can be expanded or contracted as needed.

This rugged Anker pack is one of the best affordable and reliable portable chargers you can buy. The 10,000 mAh battery has plenty of juice to recharge your smartphone multiple times, just in case the seat-back power is once again on the fritz. It also boasts ports for standard USB-A and USB-C.

This small yet mighty power pack recharges devices ludicrously fast. Better yet, an LCD screen indicates the powerbank's remaining charge percentage. Plus, it boasts the same impressive power reserve as the Anker above and supports both USB-C and USB-A.

This handy Swiss-made multitool is knife-free and carry-on-approved, so feel free to take it on board. It features a small pair of scissors, tweezers, a toothpick, a bottle opener, and a Phillips head screwdriver for good measure. 'Shoot, a fella could have a pretty good weekend in Vegas with all that stuff.'

Tangled wires make my head spin. Fortunately, these cheap, bendable cable ties exist. Durable, reusable, and also fun to fidget with, these may not be the sexiest gift, but they are ones they'll appreciate in the long run.

REI's packing cubes are expandable and compressible thanks to a zipper on the back. They're also seriously well-constructed, featuring a ripstop nylon exterior treated with a water-repellent coating. This set includes three size cubes: small, medium, and large.

This sleek and petite pack offers 2L of storage and plenty of interior pockets, along with elastic loops to keep all of your tech necessities, including cables, chargers, batteries, and more, nicely organized. The inside is also fleece-lined for added protection.

Don't waste a plastic Ziploc bag. Instead, tow your favorite bar of soap in sophisticated style with this dedicated, fold-down soap case. Beyond being reusable, duh, it's quick to dry and takes up minimal space.

Smart luggage is a smart move. The Bigger Carry-On from Away Travel features a built-in removable battery to keep gadgets charged. It's also super sleek, durable, and overhead-compartment compliant. Find out more about why we love the Away Travel Bigger Carry-On in our review.

As its name implies, the Big Haul is all about schlepping lots of stuff — 60 liters' worth, to be exact. Best of all, it can be carried as either a backpack or a duffel bag, and the straps easily tuck away when not in use. It also boasts numerous attachment points and a weather-resistant exterior.

Checking a bag? This lightweight, hard-sided spinner suitcase is tough-built and cleared for takeoff. It features two internal zippered compartments, a durable polycarbonate exterior, and the ability to expand capacity by two inches (just in case you pick up too many souvenirs). Best of all, it's also designed to survive occasional mishaps like tumbles down subway stairs.

I used to live life on the edge, packing my checked bag with reckless abandon, hoping and praying it wasn't overweight. Those days are now behind me, thanks to this tiny $10 gadget.

This minuscule speaker is waterproof, tough-built, and most importantly, big on sound. The perfect travel companion for folks who like to jam out in their hotel room, battery life is good for up to 10 hours in our testing.

The latest Amazon Kindle (2026) is the best e-reader for most people right now, with a starting price of just $149.

The latest Apple iPad Air M4 is the best overall tablet of 2026 and a great choice for travel, thanks to its lightweight (and elegant) design. It also offers great battery life, a truly stunning display, and speedy performance. For more on why we love it, head to our Apple iPad Air M4 review.

One of the most tempting holiday Nintendo Switch 2 deals is this Mario Kart World Bundle for $549. You get a Switch 2 console with two controllers and a digital copy of Mario Kart World, one of my personal favorite Switch 2 games of the past few years.

There is no Nintendo Switch 2 Lite, but the original Switch Lite can be picked up for cheap if you're looking to dip your toes into handheld gaming. It doesn't offer the same hybrid gameplay as its big brother or the Switch 2. But it plays all the same games. And for those often on the go, it may be a better choice thanks to its petite, lightweight design. Find out more in our Nintendo Switch Lite review.

Dinkey Kong Bananza is "a joy to play from start to finish thanks to the game’s destructible environments and unique visuals. It’s the 3D Donkey Kong game fans of the character have always wanted, and it lives up to the hype." Find out more in our DK Bananza review.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was easily the second-most anticipated video game release of 2026, and it definitely did not disappoint. In our full review, we called it "a joy to revisit from start to finish thanks to its gorgeous 4K visuals, full orchestral score, and slick modern controls. It may not be a brand-new adventure, but it’s the definitive remake fans have always wanted and easily the best way to experience the legendary game that started it all."

These supremely soft, lightweight, and sweat-wicking T-shirts are both my go-to for workouts and for travel. Stretchy, roomy, and odor-crushing, I make a point of picking up a few anytime they go on sale.

This lightweight, insulated synthetic jacket is the perfect mid-layer for cold-weather activities like hiking and snowboarding. It's also a good choice for those who get chilly easily on airplanes. When not being worn, the PrimaLoft Packaway does what its name suggests: it packs away into an interior zippered chest pocket. In this form, it makes for a good travel pillow.

An upgrade from the L.L. Bean puffer above, the Arc'teryx Atom Insulated Hoody is my current go-to jacket for travel thanks to a lightweight design that offers plenty of synthetic insulation, breathable fleece side panels, and a water- and wind-resistant exterior.

Fun fact: This was Houdini’s favorite jacket, hence the name. He even wore it during some of his most famous escapes. Okay, not really, but there is something magical about a packable garment that takes up almost no space, weighs next to nothing, yet provides a fair amount of weather protection.

This $100 rain jacket represents tremendous bang for the buck... I've even worn mine in the shower without getting wet. Ultimately, the Rainier will keep you dry in all but heavy and/or sustained downpours. It's also lightweight, comfortable, and breathable, all while not breaking the bank.

Keep your fingers warm and toasty with these soft-shell, wind- and weather-resistant gloves from Arc’teryx. Lightweight, comfortable, and grippy, they will serve you well when the temps drop. Toss a pair in your glovebox for chilly mornings or wear them when you take the dog out for a walk when it's four in the morning, at the end of December.

One of my favorite affordable hiking accessories, the Patagonia Sun Mask is both stylish and practical, offering 40+ UPF sun protection. Stretchy, soft, and sweat-wicking, it's perfect for keeping the sun off your neck but can also be pulled up over your head for extra protection.

While fancier hotels occasionally provide disposable slippers, I've gotten in the habit of packing my own. For less than the cost of two coffees, you and your favorite person can have cozy toes all vacation long. These travel slippers also pack flat and feature no-slip grip.

A high-quality headlamp is an invaluable piece of tech for emergencies and makes a great addition to anyone's safety kit or disaster prep pack. This affordable and well-built option provides up to 300 lumens of illumination, reaching a maximum distance of 55 meters. Battery life is good for four hours on high power and an impressive 140 hours on low.

Kiss the dreaded jumper cables and awkward pleas with strangers goodbye forever. For less than $100, an automatic jump starter is a great emergency kit addition, especially if you live somewhere cold. It can also be used to charge electronics and has a built-in LED flashlight.

Give your tired buns a rest with Purple's travel-friendly Simply Seat Cushion. It's super comfy, especially for long-haul drives, and designed to work well in most vehicles. The outer cover is machine washable, just in case you spill some coffee/ketchup/etc.

Ideal for drivers who want to avoid obstructing their view, the Garmin Dash Cam Mini 3 is the best compact dash cam in 2026 for most people. Offering Full HD video, voice control, and a tiny footprint, it's more affordable than most of the competition and less noticeable, too. Find out more in our Garmin Dash Cam Mini 3 review.

The Fanttik X8 Apex may be compact and unassuming, but it's also one of the best tire inflators in 2024. We love it for its petite size, large display, onboard battery, and built-in LED flashlight. It's also a piece of cake to use. Want to know more? Read our Fanttik X8 Apex review.

Preparation is the key to any successful trip. This is especially true when embarking on a long road trip. Whether you're driving a new car or a beloved clunker, make sure you have one of the best emergency car kits on board. The DOT Essential OSHA ANSI Compliant Kit comes in a compact duffel bag and includes many essentials like a fire extinguisher, first aid kit, emergency lights, and more.

#3497. You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.

Google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October. Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”

With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:

With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”

Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.

Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”

Powered by the new Hydrogen model, free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

#3496. Tracker & Marshals' Unexpected Schedule Change Reason Finally Revealed

Television networks frequently adjust their programming schedules throughout the broadcast season, and both Tracker and Marshals are not immune to it, despite their popularity. Some changes are more difficult to explain than others. Although temporary interruptions are hardly unusual, audiences generally expect their favorite shows to maintain consistent schedules during the fall. This is especially true for established hits that regularly attract millions of viewers and serve as anchors for their respective networks.

CBS made a particularly surprising decision in November 2026 when it temporarily removed two of its most successful Sunday night dramas from the schedule. Both Tracker and Marshals were forced to take an unexpected break, despite neither series experiencing any obvious scheduling conflicts that would justify the interruption.

Instead, CBS dedicated the evening to its freshman legal drama Cupertino, airing three consecutive episodes in place of its usual Sunday lineup. Although the decision provided the new series with additional exposure, it raised questions about why the network would disrupt two proven performers so early in the television season.

Now, CBS's newly announced 2027 midseason schedule offers a compelling explanation. What initially appeared to be an unusual promotional strategy may have actually been an opportunity to test a significant programming change before making it permanent.

Although brief interruptions are common during a television season, CBS's decision to suspend Marshals and Tracker on November 8 was particularly unusual. November is traditionally an important period for broadcast networks, with Nielsen's November sweeps encouraging networks to showcase their strongest programming. Removing two successful dramas from the lineup without an obvious scheduling conflict therefore seemed counterproductive.

Neither series was being displaced by a major sporting event, awards ceremony, or special broadcast. Instead, CBS devoted three consecutive hours to Cupertino, beginning with a new episode at 8 p.m. ET. Encore presentations of the legal drama's first two episodes followed at 9 p.m. and 10 p.m., temporarily replacing the network's established Sunday programming.

The decision was especially surprising considering the importance of both dramas to CBS. Marshals, a spinoff of Yellowstone, and Justin Hartley's Tracker have become major attractions for the network. Their popularity makes them valuable assets for maintaining consistent Sunday night viewership, especially during the competitive fall television season.

While promoting Cupertino to a larger audience offered one explanation, interrupting two of CBS's most successful shows was still a considerable gamble. The network could have used its existing Thursday programming or another available time slot to provide additional exposure. Instead, CBS deliberately positioned the freshman series where viewers ordinarily expected to find Marshals and Tracker, suggesting the decision served a larger purpose.

CBS's November 16 announcement of its 2027 midseason schedule finally provides context for the unusual programming decision. Beginning January 17, Cupertino will officially move from Thursdays to Sundays at 10 p.m. ET, airing immediately after Marshals and Tracker. Meanwhile, Matlock season 3 will inherit the legal drama's previous Thursday time slot beginning January 21.

The announcement makes November's unexpected interruption look considerably more strategic. By giving Cupertino an entire Sunday evening, CBS effectively had an opportunity to evaluate how audiences responded to the series outside its original Thursday placement. Although the November broadcast did not replicate its eventual 10 p.m. slot, it demonstrated how the freshman drama could perform on a different night.

Tracker season 4 returns after a mini-hiatus with a compelling weekly case that also finally completes a difficult transition period for the CBS show.

More importantly, the experiment appears to have produced encouraging results. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Cupertino attracted its largest audience of the season during its November 8 Sunday broadcast. CBS also indicated that the show's Sunday repeats at 10 p.m. had performed comparably to its original Thursday airings.

These results help explain why CBS would temporarily sacrifice new episodes of two established hits to promote a freshman series. The network was not simply trying to draw attention to Cupertino; the special broadcast also provided valuable information about the show's potential to strengthen its Sunday night lineup.

Additionally, placing Cupertino immediately after Tracker in January allows CBS to capitalize on the audiences already watching its two highest-profile Sunday dramas. The arrangement creates a potentially powerful three-hour scripted television block while freeing Thursday's 10 p.m. slot for Matlock.

Ultimately, the scheduling disruption now looks less like an unnecessary interruption and more like a calculated investment in Cupertino's future. While CBS has not explicitly identified the November 8 broadcast as a formal test, its subsequent scheduling decision suggests the experiment helped establish the drama's next home.

Colter Shaw travels across the country making his living by collecting missing persons rewards, utilizing sharp instincts and expert tracking skills. With help from a small support team, he works alongside private citizens and law enforcement while staying one step ahead of violent suspects.

Kayce Dutton transitions from life on the Yellowstone Ranch to joining an elite unit of U.S. Marshals in Montana. Merging his cowboy heritage and Navy SEAL expertise, he tackles the challenges of balancing family, duty, and the psychological toll of combating regional violence.

#3495. 'MobLand's Johnny Flynn on His Favorite One-on-One Scene With Tom Hardy in Season 2

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for MobLand Season 2 Episode 10.MobLand has finally reached its conclusion for Season 2, delivering an even more shocking ending than Season 1. With the Harrigans on the run and the police branding them as terrorists, the walls are closing in, and the dysfunctional family finds themselves holed up in Harry's (Tom Hardy) safe house in the middle of nowhere. As the family members begin to turn on each other, it seems like Harry has finally had enough and seemingly sells them out to Kat McAllister (Janet McTeer). When she sends Frankie Cooper (Johnny Flynn) to kill the family at the safe house, Frankie arrives to an ambush, revealing Harry's long game and putting the Harrigans back on top by the end of the season.

We spoke with Flynn about playing Frankie Cooper and what it was like filming those big one-on-one scenes across Hardy as well as talking about the hard work that goes into major action sequences like the firefight in the finale. Cooper talked about Frankie's tête-à-tête with Gina (Teddie Allen) and breaks down his final scene across from Maeve (Helen Mirren). Considering the two last worked on the Christmas movie Goodbye June together, this new setting gave Mirren and Flynn a chance to explore a new dynamic.

Before I talk about that finale, I want to talk about Episode 9 and that scene you had with Tom Hardy. Because it was such a good scene, seeing the two of you together in the pub, and seeing this different side to Harry with Frankie. What was it like filming that scene and doing more of the one-on-one character work with Tom?

JOHNNY FLYNN: I mean, I loved that scene in particular; I think it was probably one of my favorite ones to do in the show, and Tom's such a great actor. The chess playing that these guys do, it's on a level that's just thrilling as an actor to inhabit that space. They're both master chess players, but they both have very different styles, and how they're going to match up with each other, and the enjoyment of the game playing, it feels like they can see something in each other. They recognized something of their own power and darker nature in each other. In a way, they're kind of yin and yang to this same attitude, to a kind of ruthless pursuit of what they have to achieve. And it's why they're both kind of at the top of their respective organizations.

Yeah, no, it's so fun, and I loved the episode. It was nice, because you could say that Frankie gives it away a bit easily, [laughs] like, for somebody who's so smart, he seems to make some pretty dumb mistakes, but it was nice with that one, because I knew, as Johnny, that in playing the mistakes that I make in that scene, tactically they're made on purpose. I need Gina to get out, because I'm playing this master plan with Kat, and I haven't been distracted by Michael's death and everything. So all of that was really cool to contain and then unravel and reveal. And Tom's just great; he's a wonderful person, very strange, and talented, and, surprising, really, which I really love.

I think another one-on-one scene that I really enjoyed was specifically your scene with Teddie [Allen] as Gina and Frankie, in the panic room/playroom. I thought that was such an interesting reflection of both of those characters. Do you like exploring that sort of other side to his character, as opposed to just exploring the gangster?

FLYNN: Yeah, I think what's fun about Frankie is he's not an action hero. Like, I get to have some time in shootouts and things like that, but his superpower is his ability to unnerve people and his strangeness. I think the reason why he's given these wonderful moments, like with Gina, or even the long scenes with Tom's character, is that that's the stuff that he relishes, and that he's good at. He's trying to extract as much as he can; there's something kind of vampiric about him.

He's not there to just go in and shoot people; he's there to suck information and power out of people and get himself to a better position before just pulling a trigger, you know what I mean? Even with Gina, which is why that scene feels so dark, you just don't know what he wants from her, what he's gonna do with her. And Teddy's brilliant, and I really loved hanging out with her. All of it was just really fun, basically.

To talk a little bit about that finale, I was surprised to see that Frankie was still alive by the end of it, but I love getting to see you and Helen Mirren in the same scene together. What was it like filming that scene and getting to spar with Helen, even if it's just for a short scene?

FLYNN: Well, it's weird, because we've known each other for a while, and the last time I'd seen her, I'd been crying over her in a hospital bed as my dying mother, as I'm reading her poetry in a very gentle way in the film that we did last year, which was, you know, the opposite experience to playing this sweet grieving son who's losing his mother. And here she is, you know, offering to attach electrodes to my nuts.

But she's so fun. I mean, we were improvising a lot around that scene, and making jokes about the voltage going up to 11 and referencing Spinal Tap and things like that, which none of it made it [to the episode]. But I think that might have been my last day on the series; anyway, it was near the end. It was great to have that, because we obviously didn't cross over before then. We were sometimes in the same places at the same time, and got to say hi and hang out. And, gosh, she's amazing.

She's so good in the show, and then she's just the nicest person, and funny, and naughty, and lovely to be with and everything. But she's sort of saying, "Do you think I can say this? I've been given this line." I think for somebody like her to have that fun and freedom — with such an incredible, long, and respected career as she has — is lovely to see. So, it's great to be a part of it with her in the scene.

I know the show's starting back up with Season 3; can you tease whether or not we'll see you again in the show? Because I will be sad if you don't come back in Season 3.

FLYNN: I don't know, I don't know, I'm waiting to hear. I couldn't even guess at this point, but I guess, technically, it seems like I'm not actually dead at the end of the last one, but I don't know. I really have no idea.

And then, to wrap up, you guys have these really big firefight scenes where you're shooting, and there are guns everywhere, and there are a lot of stunts. What is it like filming on those types of days? Is it exhausting, or is it more somebody else's work, and you're just there for the shots where your face is involved?

FLYNN: No, it is pretty full-on. It's exhausting, like, the big firefight at the safe house. That was a whole night of... And also, because you're doing the gasping, and it's been gassed and everything. It's very physical, and I'm firing a real Uzi, firing blank shells; the shells are really flying out, because that's what they need to see. So if the camera's here, and I shoot here, the cameraman gets hit [by the shells], so you have to choreograph it really carefully, and I've fired guns and stuff, but I haven't fired a submachine gun, like, a million times.

But it's great. I love all of those aspects of the job, I really do. I like generally getting to do stuff that you don't do in real life, so that was fun. And this type of storytelling — what I love about it — it's craft, but you then hide... you kind of sprinkle the front piece of the story on top of… there's a lot of work behind that visage of what you see. Many, many people and many hours of work and thinking [go into] telling a good story, and I love that you're trying to hide the cogs and the wheels. But, yeah, it was hard work.

#3494. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3493. Segway E3 Go review: A solid midrange scooter

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Segway E3 Go is a comfortable scooter with front suspension, but it's outshone by the E3 Pro, which can be had for just $50 more, as well as the Apollo Dash, which has a rougher ride, but is better on hills.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Sometimes, you don’t need a monster of an electric scooter to get where you need to go. The Segway E3 Go is made for those with more modest demands for their commute; priced at $649 — but often on sale for less — it also places a more modest demand on your wallet.

I rode the Segway E3 Go for a couple of weeks to get a feel for this mid-range commuter scooter, and to see how it compared to some of the best electric scooters I’ve tested over the years.

The Segway E3 Go came out in 2026, and retails for $649, though you can often find it on sale for less than $500. For example, for Black Friday, it's discounted to $449 right now.

Segway has put a lot of thought into the feel of its scooters; in recent years, it’s started bending its handlebars slightly back, like on a bike, which gave me a bit more control while I was out and about.

The E3 Go’s deck is also fairly spacious; unless you have gigantic feet, you should have no trouble positioning yourself on the scooter.

I’m also a fan of the E3 Go’s folding mechanism; there’s a small tab at the base of the downtube, which you simply press with your foot to unlock the front half of the scooter and fold it down.

However, you’ll still need a bit of strength to carry it around, as the E3 Go weighs a meaty 46 pounds. The E3 Pro, which has dual suspension and a longer range, is actually six pounds lighter.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While it lacks the full suspension of its more expensive siblings like the E3 Pro, the Go still has a front suspension. It made for a much smoother ride when going over potholes and other bumps when compared with scooters that lacked such amenities.

Built into the handlebars of the E3 Go are turn signals, which you activate using a thumb switch on the left handlebar; I’ve loved this addition to all electric scooters I’ve tested. I just wish the E3 Go had rear turn signals, like the Segway Max G3 Plus, as it’s hard for cars behind you to see the handlebar signals. I also wish that the E3 Go’s headlight were slightly bigger, and that you could adjust its angle.

Like most of Segway’s scooters, the E3 Go has Apple FindMy, so you can track it if it goes missing. You should always use a lock, but it’s an extra bit of protection.

The 400W motor in the E3 Go proved good, but not great, at climbing hills. On a moderate 5% grade, the scooter slowed to around 10 MPH, which is respectable given its price; however, on a steeper hill with a 6.9% grade — which gets as steep as 10.8% — the E3 Go barely made it to the top, where the similarly-priced Apollo Dash made it up without issue. To be fair, Segway says that the E3 Go is rated to a max grade of 9% (18º slope).

Segway advertises the E3 Go as having a max range of 25 miles; if you set the scooter to its highest performance setting, that estimate drops to just 11.2 miles. I took the E3 Go out for a 5.5-mile ride, and at its conclusion it had 32% battery life remaining, which would mean I would have made it to a little over 8 miles before the battery was completely drained. Of course, your mileage will literally vary based on your weight and the type of riding you do.

The Segway E3 Go is a good, capable scooter for the price. It should be especially useful in flatter urban areas, and will suit commuters well, so long as you don’t have any major hills to climb. If you have steeper terrain, I would recommend the Apollo Dash; while its ergonomics aren’t as good, it has more power than the Segway, and costs about the same, with many other similar features.

If you can spring for the extra $50, the Segway E3 Pro has dual suspension and a longer range than the E3 Go, and is just as comfortable to ride. Either way, if you have to contend with a lot of potholes, the Segway and its suspension is worth a second look.

#3492. iCloud, App Store, and other Apple services hit by ongoing outage [U]

Apple services are having a rough Tuesday. iCloud, the App Store, and other services are experiencing an apparent outage, with users reporting connection failures and trouble signing in.

Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.

Affected services include the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone Activation, and more.

Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.

Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.

Users are reporting unexpected iCloud sign-outs on iPhone and Mac, followed by verification failures or unknown errors when trying to sign back in.

Others say the App Store won’t load or download apps, while Apple Music and device activation are also running into problems. Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect.

The number of "coincidental" system failure happening these days make it difficult to believe it's not cyberattacks, AI failures, or both. Even more suspicious is that they all seem to be reciting the same script for the cause: "an internal update".

The disruption follows last week’s widespread Microsoft Outlook outage.

Yesterday, banking services also experienced problems after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online access and delayed some transactions involving other banks.

Are Apple services working for you? Let us know what you’re seeing in the comments.

Update: Apple now says an internal update caused the outage, ruling out a cyber attack, and many services are coming back online. Consumer-facing services are back online. Developer-focused services are still experiencing issues.

Apple: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.
