Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

#3489. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3488. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

#3487. Marvel’s $2.8 Billion Masterpiece Is Officially Dominating Global Streaming Charts

Doomsday is closer than ever. The biggest cinematic event of the decade is upon us, and it's hard to keep track of exactly who is involved. The Russos have assembled their largest batch of heroes and villains yet, including Robert Downey Jr., Chris Hemsworth, Anthony Mackie, Tom Hiddleston, Florence Pugh, Vanessa Kirby, Pedro Pascal, and many more. The film is also set to be the late, great Patrick Stewart's final on-screen appearance after he sadly passed away at the age of 86 last month.

So, what's the latest update on Doomsday? The most recent news came from Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige, who promised fans a more emotionally nuanced version of Channing Tatum's Gambit, following his humor-heavy appearance in Deadpool & Wolverine. "He's a standout. It's fun to see Gambit be as charismatic as he was in Deadpool & Wolverine, and yet in Doomsday it's not all for laughs. He's a fully-rounded character."

As anticipation grows for Doomsday, Marvel's biggest movie to date is flying high on the streaming charts. Avengers: Endgame, the highest-grossing movie of all time, is currently the most-watched film on Disney+ in the world. Two of Disney's blockbuster 2026 releases, the live-action Moana movie and the fifth installment in the Toy Story franchise, are no match for Endgame right now, which also tops the Disney+ charts in the U.S. The film was a global phenomenon, scoring incredible reviews from critics, as many were left stunned that Marvel managed to pull off a seemingly impossible task.

Director James Cameron was no stranger to the #1 position at the global box office when Avatar first debuted, as it took the worldwide record from his own previous blockbuster, Titanic. Then came Endgame, which stole the title until an Avatarre-release won it back. #3486. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3484. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3483. Russell Brand Couldn't Remember Katy Perry Wedding Date During Sex Assault Case

Russell Brand's sexual history remains under the microscope ... and newly unsealed court documents include some of his jaw-dropping testimony about Katy Perry, his genitals, and an alleged assault on a movie set.

According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Brand was questioned about his marriage to Katy during a deposition tied to a lawsuit accusing him of sexually assaulting a female extra on the set of his 2011 movie "Arthur."

As Daily Mail first reported, Brand said he couldn't recall exactly when he married Katy, suggesting the information could be found online ... but he insisted during his deposition that he'd been completely faithful to her, claiming he'd redirected his sex addiction into their relationship.

The documents also detail allegations from a woman identified as Jane Doe ... who claims Brand exposed himself to her on set in July 2010 before cornering her in a bathroom and repeatedly demanding she "kiss his willy."

She alleges he then pushed her head down and forced his penis into her mouth for 5 to 8 seconds before she escaped.

Brand denied the allegations but acknowledged he couldn't completely rule out having exposed himself to someone without their explicit consent. He also insisted that, while he often used the term "willy" in an overtly nonsexual way, he would never use it for an actual sexual request.

A New York judge recently rejected Warner Bros. and other production companies' attempt to dismiss negligence claims in the lawsuit.

As TMZ previously reported ... Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in a separate UK criminal case and sentenced to 10 years and 6 months in prison. He released a message through his wife from behind bars, saying he was "not guilty."

#3481. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

#3480. 7 Classic Stephen King Books That Haven't Aged Perfectly

Okay, don’t freak out too much. The title of this whole article might look a bit incendiary, and sure, talking about these “aging badly” can be exhausting, especially when it’s not done with appropriate nuance. But the person tackling this topic does love the work of Stephen King and wants to emphasize that while many of his older books have elements that date them, most are still pretty great. There are little things here and there that date them, honestly, rather than the bunch of them being outright broken when read today, versus how they might've been experienced some decades ago.

Like, some of the Stephen King books that aren’t worth tackling are his newer ones without much that could be deemed problematic. You should read all the books below before tackling the likes of Lisey’s Story, The Colorado Kid, and Cell, for some examples. And these books were all written more than 30 years ago, and some are closer to 50 years old. Times changing and things getting dated after that long? All that’s inevitable, and interesting to think about and address, all the while still stressing that these Stephen King books are still worth tackling, and that the smaller dated elements don’t really get in the way of appreciating the good stuff. See? Nuance! You're in good hands here, don’t worry.

It’s not exactly niche in the overall scheme of things, but as far as Stephen King books go, The Talisman might qualify as a deep cut. And it’s one where King was the co-author, since Peter Straub was also credited with writing The Talisman, and then its sequel, Black House. He was credited with Other Worlds Than These (2026), which concluded the trilogy, but that was more of a solo effort on King’s part, since Straub passed away in 2022.

It villainizes some types of people a bit casually, and then the character of Speedy Parker would be written differently nowadays.

Anyway, Black House and Other Worlds Than These have technically aged “better,” and they’ve also not aged as much objectively, but The Talisman is the strongest novel of the three. It villainizes some types of people a bit casually, and then the character of Speedy Parker would be written differently nowadays (and he kind of was, when he plays a smaller role in Other Worlds Than These), but 1984 was a while ago. You can find those smaller moments a little awkward, but they're not too extreme, and they’re also a very small part of what’s ultimately a very large – and sprawling – novel.

It’s always tricky when a coming-of-age story tries to accurately portray the way kids talk. Like, once kids reach a certain age, they're potty-mouthed. You don’t always hear kids talking that way, because some avoid doing so around adults, but also, if you're an adult, obviously, you were once a kid. You were once one of those young people who refrained from swearing too much around parents and teachers, but let rip quite ridiculously around friends.

So, with The Body (a novella included in the collection Different Seasons), the kids swear a lot. That’s okay, even today, but maybe some of the slurs they use wouldn’t be included today, or if they were, the story would be more outwardly critical of such language. But you can argue it’s okay, in this instance, because these are boys who are rebelling (and doing something as daring as searching for a dead body), and further, the story’s set in the late 1950s, when things were less politically correct even compared to the early 1980s, when The Body was published. So, it’s a more minor example, but still worth noting for present purposes.

Of all the books here, Christine might be the one that feels the least essential, or the least classic, but look, it was still written early on during Stephen King’s career, at a time when he was mostly putting out bangers, and Christine definitely has its fans. It being the weakest book of the first 10 or so years of his writing career isn't really all that bad a thing when it’s got so many classics it’s up against, and in the overall scheme of things, maybe it’s still a classic.

It’s got one of those typically gonzo high-concept Stephen King premises, since it’s about a possessed car that drives two friends apart. And some other things. Christine goes off in all sorts of strange directions, and all the while, you get some stuff that hasn’t really aged all that beautifully. But it’s the same sort of “problem” you get with The Body, because it’s about young characters who aren’t really supposed to be the most considerate of people, so it more or less works (it’s more the issues with quality, regarding Christine, that make it only sort of worthy of qualifying for inclusion in this particular ranking, with the word “Classic” being in the headline and all).

There are only elements of Carrie that date it. That dating is okay when you consider the fact that it’s the oldest of King’s published novels, being his debut and all. And that sense of those small things being dated is further mitigated by the fact that the core of Carrie holds up and feels timeless, since it looks at bullying – both at school and a slightly different/more abusive sort at home – in an uncompromising way, and difficult experiences at home and school as a teenager? That’s always relevant, obviously.

It’s more the details in some smaller moments that are addressed either a bit fast or somewhat casually. There’s corporal punishment, some discomfort with Carrie casually wanting to act out violently before she actually snaps, and then even smaller things like smoking on school property. Like, yeah, you can tell it was written in the 1970s. It’s acceptable, though, and all the stuff that holds up and continues to be powerful is impressive. Some of those dated elements were why Mike Flanagan gave the world yet another Carrie adaptation in 2026; that one is decidedly more modern, and sure, intentionally doesn’t feel dated in the minor ways the original book (and the first adaptation, directed by Brian De Palma) might.

Like Carrie, Rage was a very early Stephen King book, being the first he wrote/published under his Richard Bachman pseudonym. And the books have another similarity, being set in high school and following a troubled individual who acts out in some kind of violent way, though Rage is a lot more realistic, and without supernatural elements, since that character’s a teenage boy who brings a gun to school and…

…Well, you do the math. He doesn’t go on a full-on rampage, but he commits some violence and then threatens to do more, which is where much of the tension and intentional discomfort of Rage comes in. This one’s undeniably controversial, though, since it was forward-thinking on one hand, being written before such violence in schools was as big a problem, but then a story about such a topic at all, and handled in this way, is uncomfortable in some potentially unintended ways. King himself seems to be of the opinion that Rage has aged poorly, since it’s the only Stephen King book that’s deliberately out of print (and therefore a little harder than usual to find a physical copy of).

The content is probably the biggest factor towards The Stand being a somewhat controversial Stephen King book, but then again, it is such a huge book (especially the uncut version from 1990). Also, this epic was written a while ago, so with more pages, there are going to be more opportunities for offense to be caused, and then with it being nearly half a century old, things might well be expected to feel dated.

It’s a book with a huge build-up to a conflict that involves the fate of what’s left of the world, and there’s also a lot of world-building, including some iffy stuff in terms of race and gender roles (to keep things vague, and not get bogged down in details). There’s also an extremity to some of the content of The Stand which is admittedly alarming, but at least some of it’s understandable. If you're looking at controversy more broadly, there is also the elephant in the room that is the ending to consider, but before then, and in terms of stuff that is technically dated, sure, you get a little of it throughout The Stand.

On the topic of absolutely incredible Stephen King books that are also incredibly long and quite controversial in parts, here’s IT, which has that infamous element involved in the ending, and it can’t be detailed here, but if you know, you know. As far as the basics of this one go, it’s hard to summarize the whole thing broadly, but essentially, IT is about a terrifying entity that takes on the form of all sorts of creatures and beings, including Pennywise the Clown.

And that being terrorizes people in that unbelievably cursed town of Derry every 27 years, with the main characters fighting the titular villain as kids and then as adults 27 years later, with the timelines flipped between throughout the entirety of the novel. It’s thrilling stuff, but you do get a lot here that’s very eyebrow-raising, some of it intentional and some perhaps not so much (including that aspect of the ending, which is hard to overlook and even harder to describe while keeping things “safe for work,” so to speak).

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

If you're having trouble accessing your bank right now, you aren't alone. As of Monday afternoon, a number of banks are experiencing outages and interruptions to service.

#3478. Jonathan Rinderknecht Convicted of Starting 2025 Palisades Fire

Jonathan Rinderknecht has been convicted of starting the devastating 2025 fire in the Pacific Palisades.

A jury found Rinderknecht guilty Friday during his retrial ... about 5 months after his first one ended in a mistrial.

He's been convicted on two federal charges -- one count of destruction of property by means of fire, and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

As you know, prosecutors claimed Rinderknecht set a brush fire January 1, 2025. And even though firefighters contained the initial blaze, prosecutors say it was still smoldering for days before eventually bursting into what became the Palisades fire.

Ahead of his conviction, Rinderknecht's defense had been trying to introduce new testimony from a retired Cal Fire investigator who was pointing fingers at NBA star Chris Bosh's house.

The investigator claimed to have evidence that indicated a firework was possibly set off at Bosh's home ... suggesting it could've started the blaze instead of Rinderknecht's brush fire.

But the court was unfazed by the theory ... and Rinderknecht's sentencing is set for March 17.

As you can intuit from the headline, we've got good news and bad news regarding Valve's Steam Machine.

First, the good news: Valve announced that it's worked through all of the waitlist orders for the 512GB model of the Steam Machine, and you can now purchase one for as long as supplies last. The gaming giant also finished sending out invites to the remaining reservation holders for the 2TB variant.

This is related to the bad news, but it might take a while for Valve to fulfill 2 TB requests. There are more people on that list than there are consoles available.

Yes, the Steam Machine is still expensive at $1,049, but it is finally available outside of a wishlist. Despite the price and somewhat underpowered specs, it is well-designed hardware and brings Steam OS to your couch. It's awesome for indie titles, older games and emulation.

The announcement post revealed that the company is still fighting supply constraints for hardware components, an ongoing consequence of RAMageddon.

"Even when we are able to build more, it will be at smaller quantities than we planned," the post reads. The company is also closing new signups for the waitlist.

Also, it's not clear how many 512GB Steam Machines are available for purchase. Instead of creating another waitlist, Valve says it will mark the model as out of stock.

Fortunately, as we found in September, a little hack can greatly expand your storage, so the 512GB version isn't as dire as you may think.

The Steam Machine is already more expensive than Valve wanted to price it, but high prices for RAM and storage changed the company's plans. Right now, the 512GB version starts at $1,049, while the 2TB model starts at $1,349.

Valve once again highlighted that "memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels" in this week's post.

"As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them," the company wrote. "The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained."

This suggests that a price hike is coming. Valve says that it will announce more information in January on both availability and pricing.

#3475. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3474. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

LEGO's Julia Goldin talks bringing SMART Play to Formula 1, the surprising success of its racing sets and what fans can look forward to beyond the new driver minifigures.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine building a LEGO Formula 1 car that actually sounds like one when you send it racing across your desk. Or lining up two LEGO Speed Champions cars that can interact with each other as they race.

As both a consumer technology journalist with an affinity for motorsports and an avid LEGO collector, it's something I've been thinking about since LEGO unveiled its SMART Play platform at CES in January. And now, back in Las Vegas for the 2026 Formula 1 Grand Prix, I had the opportunity to ask the person in charge of LEGO's products about it.

A post shared by Tom's Guide (@tomsguide)

I spoke with LEGO Group Chief Product and Marketing Officer Julia Goldin immediately following the reveal of the next generation of LEGO Speed Champions F1 sets.

The new collection, available March 1, 2027, recreates all 11 teams' 2026 regulation cars and introduces something fans have been waiting for: individual minifigures of all 22 drivers, complete with personalized helmets and authentic-looking race suits.

But now that LEGO has recreated the entire grid, where does the company go from here? And how might it make the experience of building and playing with these cars even more authentic?

In just two seasons, LEGO has introduced 34 Formula 1 products, some of which rank among the company's most popular offerings. And despite the enormous global appeal of motorsport, even LEGO may have underestimated the appetite for its racing sets.

“Even though we knew it was going to be successful, it still surpassed our expectations,” Goldin said.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With Formula 1 emerging as such an important part of LEGO's product portfolio, I was curious whether it could be among the next franchises to benefit from the company's investment in interactive technology.

We know that there's a lot of interest amongst the fans, so for sure we'll be looking at continually extending it to more and more lines.

LEGO's SMART Play platform has already brought a new dimension to its Star Wars and Pokémon sets, but there's arguably just as much potential for the technology in motorsport collections.

When I asked Goldin specifically about bringing SMART Play to Formula 1, her response was encouraging.

“We will be looking at it in the future as we start expanding the platform, for sure,” Goldin said.

Goldin recalled a conversation with another journalist at CES in January who had a relatively simple request for an interactive LEGO F1 car that makes noise as it drives.

“We know that there's a lot of interest amongst the fans, so for sure we'll be looking at continually extending it to more and more lines,” she said.

While Goldin stopped short of confirming that a SMART Play F1 set is in development, I'd love to see LEGO explore everything from authentic engine sounds to interactive racing experiences.

Beyond this tease towards the future, perhaps the most interesting things I learned about the success of LEGO's Formula 1 partnership is who's actually buying the sets.

“A lot of people think, oh, these would be mostly for men, but the reality is actually one of the biggest customers for F1 cars is teenage women and women in general,” Goldin said.

In 2026, the LEGO Group joined the F1 ACADEMY grid for the first time with their own F1 ACADEMY car. This set features a female F1 ACADEMY driver minifigure.

As a woman who collects LEGO and loves a good racecar, that's particularly encouraging to hear. And the company's involvement in F1 Academy, the all-female racing series, is already demonstrating how its products can serve as an entry point into the sport.

It was here in Las Vegas a year ago that LEGO announced its own F1 Academy entry, with Dutch racing driver Esmee Kosterman behind the wheel. Her No. 32 LEGO Racing car is also available as a 201-piece Speed Champions set.

According to figures shared by LEGO, its F1 Academy Speed Champions set attracts more girls than other Speed Champions sets, with one in five people who purchase it being new to F1 Academy.

I expressed my appreciation to Goldin for LEGO's investment in women's motorsport and for using its platform to give female racing drivers greater visibility.

“We have a role in society to do good,” Goldin said in response.

What I've come to appreciate about LEGO's Formula 1 partnership during my time in Las Vegas is just how much room it still has to grow.

Two seasons in, LEGO is already finding new ways to appeal to dedicated motorsport fans while giving others a reason to tune into their first race, whether that's as simple as adoring a certain driver's personalized helmet design.

For now, though, us fans have until March 1 to figure out where we're going to find the shelf space for another 11 LEGO F1 cars and 22 minifigures.

#3468. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

To read AppleInsider’s full report of Morgan Stanley’s research findings, follow this link.

#3465. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

To read WABetaInfo‘s full report, follow this link.

'The Odyssey,' Nicolas Cage in 'Madden,' 'Obsession,' and more movie night hits just landed on streaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is in full swing now, and the best streaming services are making it easy to spend these chilly evenings inside on the couch catching up on our watchlists. A ton of new movies got added this week, including several of this year's biggest blockbusters, and I'm here to shout out the marquee picks of the bunch so you can skip the scrolling and get to streaming.

For starters, Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster just landed on paid video-on-demand platforms, so you can finally watch this star-studded epic fantasy from the comfort of your own couch. Over on Netflix, you'll find one of this year's biggest horror movies that's getting Oscar buzz. Prime Video just got the perfect football season watch, and Paramount+ has all the "bah humbug!" you could ask for with Bill Murray's iconic Christmas movie performance.

So without further ado, let's dive into all the best new movies on streaming to watch this weekend.

Once you've seen one Christopher Nolan movie, you've seem 'em all, and "The Odyssey" hits all the beats you'd expect. If it were me, I'd save my $20 and wait for "The Odyssey" to come to streaming sometime early next year, but if your family is keen on watching Anne Hathaway act circles around Matt Damon and Tom Holland this holiday season, you can buy it now on the usual storefronts.

In Nolan's take on Homer’s legendary epic, Odysseus (Matt Damon) is just as tortured and lost on his perilous journey home from the Trojan War. Along the way, he and his steadfast soldiers stumble on a sheep-herding cyclops (and nobody makes any jokes), sail past wailing sirens in what's easily Damon's strongest scene in the movie, and run afoul of every beastie they can while trying to get home to his wife, Penelope (Hathaway), and son, Telemachus (Holland). The new James Bond steals the show as the slimey ringleader of Penelope's suitors who shouts about getting "these beggars out of here."

Football season is heating up, and Prime Video just added a biopic about one of the sport’s most beloved figures that's all but guaranteed to be a popular family movie night pick this holiday season. Nicolas Cage stars as the legendary coach and commentator John Madden, tracing his rise from a Super Bowl-winning partnership with Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis (Christian Bale) to becoming the voice of football for millions of fans — and the namesake of the wildly popular Madden NFL video game series.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Directed by David O. Russell ("American Hustle"), it’s a star-studded look at the man who transformed how generations of fans enjoy football, though whether it's worth your precious streaming is debatable. It's sitting at a rancid 15% on Rotten Tomatoes from critics, though audiences were warmer to it (54% on the Popcornmeter). I think the negative reviews are a bit harsh, though it takes a while for "Madden" to find its stride.

"Obsession," the supernatural horror hit starring breakout Inde Navarrette that doubles as a litmus test for crappy men based on who they think is the villain, is finally on Netflix. It racked up over $524 million at the box office, making it the highest-grossing movie Focus Features has ever released. "Obsession" deserves all that buzz too. It's a simple premise executed so well that it left me shaking in the theater. And I watch a lot of horror movies.

Navarrette puts on an iconic performance as Nikki, a young woman who suddenly finds herself more than a little obsessed with her friend, Bear (Michael Johnston), after he makes a wish on a charm called a "One Wish Willow." He doesn't expect the thing to actually work, and when it does (and in horrifying fashion), her unhinged behavior sends him scrambling to find a way to break the spell. I can't sing Navarrette praises enough — Nikki is terrifyingly unhinged, and her mood swings and outbursts might have come off as more cartoonish than chilling with a less-skilled actor. I'm excited to see how she tackles Rogue in the "X-Men" reboot.

The only "Insidious" movies I revisit regularly are the first two (which you can also find on Netflix!), but since it's a series my mom and I loved watching together, you can bet I'll be sat in the theater for every new installment. Since the last couple have been real stinkers, I didn't expect to have as much fun watching "Insidious: Out of the Further" as I did. Directed by Jacob Chase ("Come Play"), the latest chapter ditches the ghost-hunting Lambert family for Gemma (Amelia Eve), a mother raising her daughter in her childhood home. The same home where a young Gemma watched her mother kill herself while supernatural forces wreaked havoc.

After a chilling premonition, she learns she can enter the Further, the shadowy realm of lost souls that fan-favorite parapsychologist Elise (Lin Shaye) explained to us in the first movie. Drawn to Gemma's light, demons start turning our world into their own personal playground. Campy, creepy and blessedly light on jump scares, "Out of the Further" is a pleasant enough horror chiller that should please fans of the franchise. I know that dental cleaning sequence will haunt my nightmares for years to come.

Watch "Insidious: Out of the Further" on Netflix now

Instead of seeing "Ebenezer" in theaters this weekend, your time would be better spent revisiting this Bill Murray classic on Paramount+, if you ask me. This is your father's Christmas Carol, and after the Muppets version, it's probably my favorite rendition too, reimagining the classic Dickens plot as a modern fable that still hits just as hard today. Murray plays the curmudgeonly old man at the center of it all, Frank Cross, a cynical TV executive so consumed by chasing ratings that he doesn't think twice about firing an employee days before Christmas.

He's compelled to reconsider that decision when, on Christmas Eve, as he preps a live broadcast of “A Christmas Carol,” the ghost of his old mentor pays him a visit. You know the drill: Frank gets dragged through his past, present and future as one spirit after another tries to convince him to change his mean ol' ways. If the usual holiday cheer in these kinds of movies makes your teeth rot, the writing's smart-aleck bite and Murray's sneering meanness make "Scrooged" a nice palette cleanser.

#3462. 6 Children's Books That Are Better Than Harry Potter

J. K. Rowling began writing her debut novel, the tale of a young orphan magician named Harry, around the summer of 1990. After five years, the book finally came together as Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (which would later be published in the US as Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone). After several publishers kept rejecting the initial manuscript, the eight-year-old daughter of Bloomsbury's chief executive fell in love with Rowling's writing so deeply that the publisher decided to add this to their growing portfolio of fantasy children's literature by new writers.

The rest is history. Philosopher's Stone was a smash hit and a cultural phenomenon, sparking an equally successful book series and eventually leading the Harry Potter franchise to becoming one of the biggest multimedia franchises in the history of commercial entertainment. However, there are six particular children's books from throughout history that are even better than the Harry Potter book series as a whole. From foundational classics like The Little Prince to more relatively modern masterpieces like The Golden Compass, these absolute masterpieces are arguably the very best of the best when it comes to children's literature.

Inspired by his real-life experiences as an aviator and his longing for home and childlike wonder during World War II, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote the children's novella The Little Prince while living in New York away from occupied France. In it, a stranded desert pilot befriends a young prince from a tiny asteroid who's looking for a way back to the rose he left behind. At less than 100 pages in length, it's a remarkably easy book to read in its entirety in one sitting; but even though it was undoubtedly written for children, it's such a timeless and universally appealing masterpiece that everyone with the ability to read should check it out at least once.

Everyone is able to draw a different message from it depending on what stage of life they're at when reading it.

What's more, a single read-through will likely not be enough, since this is one of those classic books worth reading over and over again. The prose is beautiful, the emotional sincerity is remarkable, and the book's philosophical core makes it so that everyone is able to draw a different message from it depending on what stage of life they're at when reading it. Needless to say, it's significantly less vast and ambitious than an entire seven-book MG and YA fantasy book series, but its thematic depth is more existential and universal, its narrative economy is more admirable, and its easier re-readability makes it arguably superior to Harry Potter.

American writer and essayist E. B. White was best-known for his work in children's literature, and even though Stuart Little is probably what his name is most often immediately associated with, Charlotte's Web is not to be underappreciated. It's the tale of the titular barn spider, who cleverly weaves messages into her web to make a runt pig famous and save him from being slaughtered. It's easily one of the best children's books of all time, directly informed by White's own struggles raising animals that would eventually be slaughtered at his farm in Maine.

What makes Charlotte's Web so wonderful and timeless is White's refusal to condescend to his young audience, crafting a story whose emotional honesty, lyrical prose, and quiet philosophical weight make it deeply endearing regardless of the reader's age. There's zero bloat here, every moment being written with maximum emotional and thematic impact in mind. Though Harry Potter's classic brand of "Chosen One" heroism has a charm of its own, the way Charlotte's Web celebrates quieter and more ordinary kindness is arguably even more special.

There are remarkably few fantasy books more influential than Harry Potter, but there's one in particular that can be traced back as far as the mid-19th century: Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. Back in its time, the book was absolutely revolutionary for how it broke away from the contemporary children's literature tradition of moralizing to kids. Never before had a children's book been so preoccupied with entertaining its readers and purely cultivating their imagination, and the genre was never the same again as a result.

Inspired by Alice Liddell, a 10-year-old girl who Carroll entertained during a fateful 1862 boat trip, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is one of the most deliciously absurd and surreal children's books ever written, which only adds to its timeless entertainment value. With an exquisitely creative and twisted use of language, a limitless use of his imagination, and a clever subversion of adult authority, Carroll broke new ground in children's literature, paving the way for books like Harry Potter to exist in the first place. It doesn't really have much of a plot, but that's precisely where its inimitable charm comes from.

Where the revolutionary work of his dear friend J. R. R. Tolkien was the most influential and groundbreaking work of the 20th century in the field of general fantasy literature, C. S. Lewis wrote one of the most foundational children's fantasy novels of the 20th century: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, the first chapter in the iconic Chronicles of Narnia. In it, four evacuated siblings during World War II are transported to a magical winter world through a wardrobe in a house in the English countryside, where they find themselves having to ally themselves with the lion Aslan to overthrow the White Witch.

A masterpiece which completely changed the portal fantasy subgenre forever.

The result of such a premise is one of the most essential classic fantasy books to read before kicking the bucket, a masterpiece which completely changed the portal fantasy subgenre forever. It's one of the most direct literary ancestors of the kind of epic, good-versus-evil brand of children's fantasy that would eventually birth Harry Potter, and it's every bit as much of a must-read—or perhaps even more so. Full of mythic wonder and bolstered by a universally endearing Christian allegory of sacrifice and grace, it's a masterclass in warm and meaningful writing for children, which it achieves in under 200 pages.

Northern Lights (published as The Golden Compass in North America and a few other regions) is the inaugural chapter in Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials series, one of the most important and foundational in the history of '90s fantasy literature. It's one of the most essential fantasy books of the 1990s, telling the tale of a fierce young girl journeying into the Arctic to rescue kidnapped children and uncover the dark secret behind a mysterious substance called Dust. Inspired by classic literature, philosophy, and visual art, Pullman wrote the story around themes of growing up and questioning authority.

Pullman didn't actually write the book specifically for children (which probably explains the overtly anti-organized-religion attitudes that have made the novel so controversial throughout the years), but rather as a tonally and thematically layered story for all ages. But even though the book has been embraced as a classic of children's and YA literature mostly for marketing purposes, one thing is certain: Few books compare to The Golden Compass. Full of philosophical depth and intellectual ambitiousness, complete with an absolute gut-punch of an ending, it's the kind of book that all those who think Harry Potter is the best that children's literature has to offer should read.

Before its sequel became the most important fantasy novel of the entire 20th century almost a couple of decades later, The Hobbit became an absolute smash hit in 1937, immediately establishing J. R. R. Tolkien as a household name. It's the story of the home-loving hobbit Bilbo Baggins embarking on a treasure-hunting adventure with a powerful wizard and 13 dwarves, and it just so happens that it has only gotten better with age. It's one of the bestselling fantasy books in history and one of the most widely celebrated and studied classics of 20th-century children's literature, the kind of pop-cultural institution so influential that anyone who loves speculative fiction should consider it an absolute must-read.

On top of being one of the best cozy fantasy books of all time, The Hobbit is genuinely one of the most perfect fantasy novels ever written. It's the foundational bedrock of modern fantasy, a traditional Hero's Journey tale elevated by a masterful pace, beautiful prose, and Tolkien's unmatched sense of depth in terms of world-building and plotting alike. It's almost unfair to compare any other fantasy children's book to it, but if one were to put it side by side with the Harry Potter series, it would have to be the clear winner. It's tightly structured, full of masterful world-building and memorable characters, wonderfully written almost as though it were a magical piece of folklore, and brilliant in how it subverts the Chosen One trope by having an ordinary hobbit be its hero.

#3460. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link.

Be sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the Apple HomeView.

If you've ever struggled to keep a project organized or stay on top of a seemingly endless stream of emails, this could be one of the most useful ChatGPT upgrades yet.

Think of ChatGPT Space as a digital workspace that combines some of the best features of Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and Notion with the intelligence of ChatGPT.

Rather than digging through old conversations to find something ChatGPT created, you can organize your work in one dedicated location.

At the heart of Space is a feature called Pages. These interactive documents can include text, images, charts, tables and even interactive tools. You can edit them yourself, ask ChatGPT to make changes or invite other people to collaborate.

You can also turn an existing ChatGPT conversation into a page without starting from scratch.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

One of the biggest frustrations with using AI for productivity is that the information it generates can quickly become outdated.

ChatGPT Space aims to solve that problem with automated document updates. You can tell ChatGPT what information to update, which connected apps to consult and how frequently to check them.

A weekly family planner that incorporates school announcements and upcoming appointments.

A daily to-do list that pulls action items from your emails.

A vacation itinerary that reflects new booking confirmations.

A job search tracker that incorporates responses from potential employers.

A project dashboard that reflects the latest conversations in Slack.

Instead of repeatedly asking ChatGPT for the same information, you can return to an existing document to review what's changed.

OpenAI is also bringing ChatGPT Slides to Space. Powered in part by Imagegen 2.6, the feature lets you create polished presentations, collaborate with others and ask ChatGPT to incorporate feedback.

Additionally, ChatGPT generates editable charts rather than static chart images. You can modify individual elements, export your presentation to PowerPoint and edit the underlying chart data in Excel.

For anyone who's ever spent an entire afternoon tweaking a PowerPoint presentation, this alone could make Space worth exploring.

You can start with a blank page, choose a template or turn an existing conversation into a document.

Try giving ChatGPT a prompt like this: Create a weekly personal dashboard with my upcoming commitments, outstanding tasks and important emails. Set it up to refresh every Monday morning using my connected apps.

You'll need to connect the relevant services and configure the recurring updates.

While much of the competition between ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude focuses on which AI model is smarter, Space now seems like a step toward making AI more useful in everyday life.

I'm particularly interested in the potential for documents that stay current without requiring constant attention. As someone who uses AI every day, I rarely struggle to create a to-do list, research document or project plan, but keeping it all organized is a different story. Have you tried this new feature yet? Let me know in the comments what you think and how you're using it.
